title: Six Charts to Explain the Global Energy Crisis
gist: CSIS charts show the Iran war's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz (from Feb 28, 2026) sent Brent from ~$70 to $145 in April before settling near $90, cushioned by a 400mb IEA reserve release, Saudi/UAE Red Sea rerouting, surging US crude/LNG exports and a 32% cut in Chinese imports; risks ahead include SPR refills, Europe's gas storage at just 68%, a delayed LNG glut (now 2028), and helium supply shifts toward US suppliers for Asian chipmakers.

insights.claim: The Iran conflict beginning with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, 2026 effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carries 25% of seaborne crude and about 20% of LNG.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The largest energy chokepoint disruption in decades sets the backdrop for oil, LNG and product markets.
insights.locator: The six charts in this analysis

insights.claim: Brent rose from about $70/bbl in February to $145 in April and settled around $90 by end-August, far less than feared given 1973 and 1979 analogues.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Market has priced substantial mitigation; renewed disruptions could reprice sharply higher from ~$90.

insights.claim: The IEA secured pledges for a 400-million-barrel strategic reserve release, with about 290 million barrels released by end-July, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE rerouted exports via the Red Sea at 5.0 mb/d and 4.3 mb/d by June; Iraq trucked about 1,000 tankers a day through Syria to Baniyas.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Buffers are finite and partly spent; Red Sea routing is vulnerable to Houthi attacks.
insights.locator: In March, the IEA secured commitments

insights.claim: EU, US and other strategic reserves will need refilling in a tight market, which will drive crude prices higher.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: SPR restocking is a latent demand source supporting crude prices into 2027.
insights.quote: competing for supply in a tight market, driving crude prices ever higher

insights.claim: Houthi attacks in September further damaged Saudi energy infrastructure, constraining exports through the Yanbu (East-West) pipeline and the Red Sea.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The main Hormuz bypass is itself under attack—upside risk to oil prices.

insights.claim: The US entered the war exporting 3.9 mb/d of crude and 6.6 mb/d of refined products, and exports surged to fill gaps, enabled by the shale revolution, Gulf Coast pipelines, refining capacity and export terminals.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US refiners, exporters and Gulf Coast midstream benefit from wide international spreads.
insights.locator: 2. U.S. Exports of Crude Oil Jumped

insights.claim: Asia's share of US LNG exports rose from about 12% in January to about 40% in May after Iranian strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan facility, with US LNG plant utilization peaking above 100% in March before shipping and maintenance constraints cut it by summer.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US LNG exporters gain pricing power and Asian offtake; vessel availability is a constraint.
insights.locator: 4. U.S. LNG Exports Shift to Asia

insights.claim: BloombergNEF says the Iran conflict pushed the expected global LNG oversupply from 2027 to 2028, turning a projected 1.7 Mt surplus into a 3.3 Mt shortage in 2027, while repairs delay Qatar's North Field expansion by three to five years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports LNG prices and US LNG project economics for another year; delays the anticipated LNG glut.

insights.claim: China, holding nearly 1.4 billion barrels of commercial and government crude stocks, cut imports about 32% from 11.6 mb/d in 2025 to 8.0 mb/d; its imports rose again in July and August, which may tighten global supply.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China's restocking is a key swing factor; rising Chinese imports are a bullish crude signal.

insights.claim: China's ability to sustain deep import cuts is a key determinant of how long the global economy can withstand Hormuz disruptions, and its swing-consumer role may complicate US economic goals at the September 24 Trump-Xi summit.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China's stockpile gives Beijing leverage in trade talks and over oil prices.
insights.locator: China’s ability to maintain these deep cuts

insights.claim: Japan's crude imports from Saudi Arabia and the UAE fell nearly 66% to 853,329 b/d in April, and in May Japan agreed to cooperate with South Korea on procurement and swaps, importing more North American crude.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Durable Asian diversification toward North American crude supports US export flows.
insights.locator: In April, Japan’s imports of crude

insights.claim: Europe delayed refilling gas storage hoping for lower prices and has filled only 68% versus an 80% winter target, facing the heating season with gas prices as high as December 2022 and reduced pipeline supply from Algeria and Norway.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: High risk of winter European gas price spikes; bullish TTF volatility and LNG exporters, bearish energy-intensive European industry.
insights.locator: After the end of the 2025–26 heating season

insights.claim: Europe's plan to end Russian pipeline gas by November 1, 2027 depends on affordable LNG, and elevated LNG costs may slow Europe's economy and delay that phase-out.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch for slippage in EU's Russian gas phase-out and weaker European growth.
insights.locator: Europe also needs to refill its natural gas storage

insights.claim: Qatar supplied about one-third of world helium, mostly to Asian AI-chip makers; after the Gulf shut-in and Russia's partial helium export ban in April, South Korea's share of US helium rose from 28% to 56% and Taiwan's from under 4% to around 60%.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Helium is a hidden semiconductor supply risk; US gas processors gain a strategic byproduct market.

insights.claim: Samsung and SK Hynix signed long-term helium supply contracts in April with US suppliers Air Products and Linde to reduce supply risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Positive for Air Products and Linde contract volumes and pricing power in helium.
insights.locator: To reduce supply-side risk, Samsung and SK Hynix
